That level of consistent support has allowed us to stabilize operations, invest in our staff, and continue delivering high-quality educational

opportunities for our students. It's also important to acknowledge that as a board, none of you have had to go through a budget reconciliation process. Full funding in recent years does not insulate us from the financial pressures before us. Enrollment changes, rising costs, and broader economic conditions are shifting the landscape. We are entering a phase where sustainability, prioritization, and return on investment must guide our decisions more than ever. Tonight's discussion is about building on that strong foundation while also preparing for what comes next, ensuring that the decisions we make are aligned, transparent, and

sustainable for the long term. I look forward to walking you through where we are, what we're seeing ahead, and how we can continue to make responsible student-centered decisions together. I want to highlight an important aspect of how we manage our finances at LCPS. Our budget work is not a single once-a-year process. It is continuous, and it operates across two parallel year-round cycles.First, we have our operating budget cycle.

This is what most people think of when they hear the budget. It supports the day-to-day functioning of the school division from staffing, instructional programs, transportation, utilities, and the services that directly impact students in classrooms. Within the operating budget, there are multiple funds that serve a specific purpose, and together they make up the full picture of our annual operations. At the same time, we are managing a capital budget cycle. This is focused on our long-term investments in facilities,

maintaining, repairing, and renovating our existing schools, as well as addressing infrastructure needs to ensure safe, efficient learning environments. Given that we are not currently experiencing significant enrollment growth, our capital focus is less on building new schools and more on stewardship of the assets that we already have. Like the operating side, the capital program also includes multiple funds, each aligned to different types of projects. These two cycles run concurrently and are connected.

Decisions we make in the capital budget, such as major renovations or system upgrades, can have direct and lasting impacts on the operating budget through ongoing maintenance and operational costs. Understanding that we are always managing both of these processes at once is key. It reinforces the complexity of our financial planning and the importance of taking a comprehensive long-term view as we make decisions.

I also want to emphasize that our work on the FY28 budget is already underway. While it may feel a little early, this reflects the continuous nature of our budget development process and the level of thought required to plan responsibly. We have already begun internal reviews of our base budget, taking a close look at ongoing operations, core programs, their return on investment, and historical spending trends. This is a critical step in ensuring that what

we are currently funding continues to align with our priorities and is delivering value for our students. This includes perspectives from staff, leadership, and the community to help inform our thinking as we move forward. You'll also see that we are actively reviewing and refining our budget book and presentation materials to strengthen how we communicate financial information.

This work is intentionally aligned with the standards established by ASBO and GFOA for distinguished budget awards, with an emphasis on clarity, transparency, and clearly connecting resources to student outcomes and organizational priorities. If you look back at prior budget books and presentations, you will notice a steady evolution in both structure and content. possible, while still providing the appropriate level of detail in the budget book for those who want to go deeper. The team is continuing this work by valuing what is most helpful to

stakeholders, reducing unnecessary complexity, and improving visual presentation and narrative explanations so that the budget tells a clear, more coherent story about priorities, investments, and impact. And finally, we are being intentional about planning for ongoing collaboration with the school board throughout both the operating and capital budget development processes. Before we get into the specific numbers, I want to take a moment to introduce why we're shifting to a multi-year forecast and what it represents for our budgeting approach. Historically, much of our focus has been on building and balancing a single-year budget. That approach worked in a period of enrollment growth and consistent funding increases. But as we've discussed, we are now entering a new era of budgeting, one defined by slower or declining revenue growth, increasing cost pressures, and the need for long-term sustainability.

A multi-year forecast allows us to look beyond just the next fiscal year and begin to understand the trajectory of our financial position over time. It helps us identify not just whether we are balanced today, but whether the decisions we make today remain sustainable two, three, or four years down the road. This is an important shift. It moves us from a primarily annual decision-making model to a more strategic, forward-looking approach. One that highlights financial imbalances

earlier and gives us more time to plan. What you're about to see is an initial simplified version of that forecast. It is not meant to predict the future with precision, but rather to illustrate the direction we are heading under a defined set of assumptions. And with that context, I will now walk you through the model. For this slide, we are looking at a simplified multi-year forecast for the

operating fund, designed to illustrate the financial pressures ahead. As a reminder, we typically focus on the change in revenues and expenses from one year to the next, not the entirety of the $2 billion operating fund budget. To keep this as clear as possible, this model isolates just two key variables: additional county funding and new compensation costs. Everything else is held constant.

There are no assumed changes, positive or negative, in state or any other revenue streams. Additionally, there is zero net FTE growth. Any reductions in some areas are assumed to offset increases in others, such as special education.Also, flat operation maintenance costs are assumed, where we assume inflationary pressures are absorbed within existing resources.

And also that there is no additional subsidy transfer included for school nutrition. from 101.3 million of new additional county local tax funding for LCPS in FY28, reducing down to 77.6 million by FY31. On the expense row, we are modeling only compensation increases based on minimum requirements in the collective bargaining

agreement for FY28 and FY29, and then continuing those assumptions into FY30 and FY31. That includes an annual step increase and a 2% COLA. In addition, we've built in rising health insurance costs with projected premium increases of 14% in FY28 that declines down to an 8% increase in FY31. When you bring those two lines together, the picture becomes clear.

In FY28 and 29, you could see that we still would maintain a positive balance to be able to fund other investments, but that by FY30, you can see that those numbers turn red and we start anticipating a shortfall. It's, again, important to emphasize that this is not a full forecast, but even with these limited variables, it highlights the imbalance that begins to emerge. The takeaway, though, is that even under very controlled assumptions,

compensation growth alone begins to outpace projected revenue. That reinforces the need for early planning, thoughtful prioritization, and a clear strategy for long-term sustainability. And finally, adding one more important layer of context, our enrollment is projected to decline over the same period. We are anticipating a decrease from 79,896 students budgeted in FY28 down to 77,914 in FY31, per the

most recent CIP. That represents a decline of about 2.5% over this timeframe. Because our funding is closely tied to student enrollment, this reduction also results in corresponding decreases in revenue over time. While the change is gradual, it further reinforces the downward pressure on available resources and adds to the imbalance shown in this forecast. Next on this slide, we build on this scenario.

And for this next phase, the budget team looked at a range of scenarios, both low and high, to understand the potential variability in revenues and expenditures. This scenario-based approach provides a more complete view of possible financial outcomes and helps us better frame the uncertainty in the multi-year outlook. This particular slide focuses on the high forecast scenario, which incorporates more favorable revenue assumptions and additional

variability in costs and establishes the starting point for our FY28 budget development. On the revenue side, we are adding a non-county funding stream, which includes potential increases in state aid and other revenue streams. budget. This provides a more complete view of anticipated state funding in that cycle. This high scenario further reflects positive trend assumptions for sales tax and other revenue sources. Overall, non-county revenue increases from 9.5 million in FY28 to just under 27 million in FY31, reflecting a more favorable funding environment. On the expense side, though, we are

incorporating two additional factors that are often experienced as we build out the official budget, but were not included in the baseline model shown on the previous slide. First, we are adding incremental base operating costs, including increases in substitutes and overtime. Subs historically increase year over year, and with the additional leave provisions included in the collective bargaining agreement, we anticipate the need for even more subs. Overtime increases also would

be a factor based on the base pay of employees increasing. These are areas that tend to fluctuate with staffing coverage needs and operational demand. Second, we are removing the assumption from the first scenario of flat operations and maintenance and have applied annual inflationary increases on our operating and maintenance accounts. This adjustment reflects the reality that non-compensation costs such as utilities, supplies, and contractor services also continue to rise year over year.

Combined, these additional base expenditures grow modestly over time from 29 million to 31.7 in FY31. When these additional variables are incorporated, they demonstrate how sensitive the overall position is to changes outside of the core assumptions. Even with stronger non-county revenue growth, the addition of more realistic operating cost pressures materially impacts the long-term outlook and further emphasizes the imbalance that we are projecting.
